did_you_know.text: Did you know? The King of Arad, mentioned here, was the ruler of an important city in the Negev desert whose ancient remains still exist today.
Did you know? The name "Hormah," given to the place, expresses the concept of "herem" – the utter destruction of the enemy as part of a vow to God.
Did you know? The phrase "the soul of the people was impatient on the way" describes great weariness, frustration, and loss of patience from the long and difficult journey through the desert.
Did you know? The people called the manna "the despicable bread," an extreme expression indicating deep ingratitude, even though the manna had sustained them in the desert.
Did you know? The "fiery serpents" were likely named that way because of the burning effect of their venom, or perhaps due to their bright, fiery color.
Did you know? The bronze serpent, intended to heal the Israelites, was preserved for centuries until King Hezekiah had to destroy it because people began to worship it as an idol.
Did you know? "The Book of the Wars of the Lord" is one of the earliest references in the Bible to an external, non-biblical historical document, suggesting the existence of other historical records.
Did you know? The "Song of the Well" is one of the few passages in the Torah that describes a full communal song, praising the finding of water in the desert and the leaders who assisted in it.
Did you know? The "King's Highway" was a vital ancient trade route that ran through Transjordan, and Israel's request to use it highlights its strategic importance.
Did you know? Heshbon was the capital city of Sihon, King of the Amorites, and its capture by Israel symbolized their takeover of a strategic area in Transjordan.
Did you know? The poem quoted in these verses is likely an ancient Amorite victory song about Sihon's earlier conquest of Moab, showing their regional power even before Israel's arrival.
Did you know? Og, King of Bashan, was famous for his immense height, described elsewhere in the Bible as one of the last of the Rephaim, an ancient race of giants.
